title: Eighty-three at two minutes
objective: Recognize exercise-induced desaturation on a walk test (a fall in SpO2 of more than 4% is clinically significant; desaturation below 80% is the commonest reason to stop)
secondaryObjectives: Titrate supplemental oxygen to target saturations: 94% to 98% for most patients, 88% to 92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, such as COPD

brief.situation: 09:00 in an outpatient pulmonary rehabilitation gym. You are the physical therapist doing Mr. Lindqvist's intake 6-minute walk test on room air. His resting SpO2 is 93%. His pulmonologist's referral includes an order to titrate oxygen to a saturation of 88-92% during exercise.
handover: He has a history of hypercapnic respiratory failure two winters ago.

Clinic policy: stop a walk test for a stopping rule, rest seated, titrate oxygen under the referral's order, and tell the pulmonologist the same day when exertional desaturation needs an ambulatory oxygen prescription.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What did Mr. Lindqvist's walk test show, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: A fall from 93% to 83% is clinically significant exertional desaturation (more than 4 points) and below the stopping floor; with prior hypercapnic failure his target is 88-92%.
parts.modelAnswer: He dropped 10 points, from 93 to 83, which is significant and under the floor, so the test stops. With his history of hypercapnic failure, his target's 88 to 92, not higher.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stops and seats him, titrates oxygen to 88-92% under the order, records the details and tells the pulmonologist for an ambulatory prescription.
parts.modelAnswer: Stop, sit him down, titrate oxygen to 88 to 92, write it all down and call the pulmonologist for ambulatory oxygen.

scoring.modelReasoning: During a walk test a fall in SpO2 of more than 4% is clinically significant, and desaturation below the floor is a reason to stop. Mr. Lindqvist fell from 93% to 83% at 2 minutes. Stop and seat him, titrate oxygen under the referral's order to 88-92% (his prior hypercapnic respiratory failure puts him in that group; 94-98% applies to most others), record time, distance, lowest SpO2 and Borg, and tell the pulmonologist the same day for an ambulatory oxygen prescription.
